english.html: triumvirate, Toranius had sold two young boys as twins, because they were altogether alike, although the one was from France and the other from Asia. Which being discovered by M. Antony, who had paid three hundred sesterces for them, coming to three thousand seven hundred and fifty écus of our money (for the sesterce, according to the reckoning of Budé and other learned persons, reduced to the money of France, was worth about twenty-five écus, which, multiplied three hundred times, comes, a little more or less, to the said sum of 3,750 écus), he was at first sight a little vexed by it; but Toranius showed him that the thing he complained of ought to be esteemed by him the most precious part of his purchase. For if the children had been twins, there would have been nothing marvellous in their being alike, since they would have been begotten of one and the same seed, under the same stars and constellations; but to see two children born of different parents, in different countries, and so far apart, the one in Asia, the other in Europe, was a prodigious and greatly astonishing thing. With which answer Mark Antony was so well content that he was wont to say that in all the greatness of his possessions he had nothing so dear nor so precious as these two boys <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. Once in Sicily there was a fisherman so like Sura, a Roman, at that time proconsul there, that they were alike not only in bodily resemblance but also in manner of speech, for both were stammerers. To whom Sura once said in jest that he greatly marvelled how he came to be so like him, seeing that my father (said Sura) was never in this country — meaning thereby to tax the honour and chastity of the poor fisherman's mother; who nonetheless did not show himself a dolt in answering him, saying that Sura had no cause to marvel at it, for his own father had often been at Rome: throwing back by this means upon Sura's mother what Sura had wished to stamp upon his own <sup class="mk" data-key="f">f</sup>. Sebastian Münster, a man of great reading, relates in his Cosmography that after the third defeat of the Burgundians by the Swiss (in which their Duke Charles was killed), which was about the year one thousand four hundred and seventy-seven, there came a man to Bruxelles, a town of the diocese of Speyer, who so naturally resembled the late

notes.citation: Pliny, Natural History VII.10 (§56); Solinus as above
notes.gloss: Toranius the slave-dealer and the pretended twins, one born in Gaul (Coras: France), one in Asia. Pliny gives the price as 200,000 sesterces (ducentis HS); Coras's "three hundred sesterces" reckoned at 25 écus each are in fact sestertia, units of a thousand, as Budé's De asse computes them.

notes.citation: Pliny, Solinus and Valerius Maximus at the places cited; the fisherman of Sicily who resembled the proconsul Sura is Valerius IX.14 (fragment number unverified)
notes.original: Pline, Solin, & Valere aux lieux que deſſus
notes.gloss: The retort "my father was often at Rome" is also told of Augustus and a young provincial in Macrobius, Saturnalia II.4.20.

uncertain.note: 'l'année' is set with a visible gap before the final e ('l'anné e'), which at reading size looks like two words. At native resolution it is one word loosely spaced; normalized to 'l'année' per §1.

spacing: the compositor repeatedly sets a comma or colon with no following space ('ces,reuenans', 'moins,à', 'tant,ne', 'mence,ſous', 'Rome:reiettant', 'Suiſſes:qui', 'Munſter,homme') and sometimes a space before a mark ('d'Aſie .', 'parens ,en', 'pays ,', 'parler .', 'admirable .', 'ieu ,'). All normalized to single spaces per §1; nothing added or removed beyond spacing. Parentheses likewise: '(car', 'eſcus)il', 'tué)fai' are set tight and normalized.

five line breaks are printed with no word-break hyphen and are transcribed as printed: lines[3] 'ſeſter' + lines[4] 'ces'; lines[18] 'reſpon' + lines[19] 'ſe'; lines[35] 'deſconfitu' + lines[36] 're'; lines[36] 'fai' + lines[37] 'te'. Hyphens are printed normally elsewhere on the page ('en-', 'redu-', 'eſ-', 'ſe-', 'cho-', 'pa-', 'a-'), so these are compositor omissions, not lost ink. Per §1 no entry is strictly required; recorded for the reconciler.

the final letter before the point is at the limit of the scan. Compared side by side with the certain italic x of 'aux lieux' in this same note and in note f, the two glyphs are near-identical in shape, so the letter could be an x. Read as z because 'prealleguez' is a word and 'prealleguex' is not. Reader B may read 'prealleguex.' or 'preallegués.'.

'ne:' — two dots are stacked after 'ne' (the continuation of 'Pli-|ne'), so a colon is transcribed. Note f gives the same citation formula without any mark after the author names, so this could be a point with a speck above it.
the capital of 'Valere' (Valère Maxime) is the italic swash form, which in this font reads as either V or U. Transcribed V from the name.
no point is printed after the final 'deſſus', or it is lost at the edge of the type; transcribed as printed. Note e ends with a clear point.
the head is set in spaced capitals and is closed up here per §3. It ends with a point, matching the conventions' recto example.

no signature, no catchword and no foot citation block are printed. The leaf is blank from just below the last body line to the foot of the page (checked on foot.jpg, which shows the untrimmed bottom margin), so nothing is lost to the crop.

only two margin notes on the page, keyed e and f, and both markers are present in the body (lines[21] and lines[34]). The alphabet therefore runs a–d on the preceding pages of this annotation and continues past f on the next; nothing is missing here.
